questions.question_stem: The phone holds a key, the note "Pay Alice 1 BTC" and a valid signature on it. Does that prove its owner, Smith, paid Alice?
questions.correct_answer: No: it proves the phone's key signed that note, at High confidence; who used the key is evidence still to find.
incorrect_answers: Yes: a valid signature proves the owner approved the note, so Smith paid Alice, and High confidence fits that well.
No: a valid signature proves nothing, since anyone can forge one without the key, so the note rates only Low.
Yes: the key sits on Smith's phone, so the chain names Smith as the sender, though at Moderate confidence.
questions.explanation: The review answers the opening case: the phone proves the key signed the note and controls two addresses, at High confidence. Who used the key is the agent's evidence to find, not something the signature shows.

questions.question_stem: A digest found on a phone is the SHA-256 of a short payment note. Why can an analyst still find the note without reversing the hash?
questions.correct_answer: Payment notes come from a small set of likely texts, so hashing each candidate until one matches finds it.
incorrect_answers: SHA-256 leaks a message's length and opening words, so the note can be rebuilt from those clues in its digest.
Pre-image resistance protects only long inputs, so a short note can be read straight out of its own digest.
A hash is a form of encryption, so the note comes out once the phone's key is used to decrypt the digest.
questions.explanation: A digest cannot be reversed, only matched. When the input came from a small set, an attacker hashes every candidate until one matches, which is how the note falls.
questions.lesson_block: You cannot run a hash backwards, only guess

specific_source.anchor: You cannot run a hash backwards, only guess

questions.question_stem: The digests of "Pay Alice 1 BTC" and "Pay Alice 2 BTC" share no pattern a reader can see. What does that teach about comparing IDs?
questions.correct_answer: Compare the whole string, or let a tool do it, because a digest says nothing about how close two inputs were.
incorrect_answers: Compare the first and last few characters, because digests of nearly identical inputs almost always share a prefix.
Compare only the first characters, because a changed input alters the part of the digest that depends on it.
Compare the digests' lengths, because a one-character change in the input makes its digest longer or shorter.
questions.explanation: The avalanche effect means one changed bit flips about half the output bits, so similar digests do not mean similar inputs. Check the whole ID, or let the tool compare it.

questions.question_stem: An analyst checks an Ethereum address with an online "SHA3-256" tool and the digest does not match. What is the likely cause?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum uses Keccak-256, which gives different digests from NIST's SHA3-256, so the tool used the wrong hash.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum builds addresses with SHA-256 and then RIPEMD-160, as Bitcoin does, so no SHA3 tool can match one.
Keccak-256 and SHA3-256 are one hash under two names, so the analyst must have mistyped the address.
Ethereum hashes each address twice with Keccak-256, so a tool that hashes only once gives another digest.
questions.explanation: Keccak-256 is not SHA3-256: NIST changed the padding before publishing SHA3, so the two differ for the same input. A tool labelled SHA3 may mean either.
questions.lesson_block: Each chain picks its hash; Ethereum's is Keccak

specific_source.anchor: Each chain picks its hash; Ethereum's is Keccak

questions.specific_source_lesson: 04-CP-asymmetric_encryption_and_digital_signatures.qmd: Each chain picks its hash; Ethereum's is Keccak

questions.question_stem: An agent asks the analyst to decrypt a digest found on a phone to see what was paid. What is the right answer?
questions.correct_answer: A hash has no key to decrypt with; the input can only be found by guessing candidates and hashing each one.
incorrect_answers: A hash is decrypted with the sender's public key, but that key must first be recovered from the seized phone.
A hash can be decrypted once its length is known, because a fixed length reveals the input length.
A hash can be neither undone nor matched, so a guess-and-check search will never find the original input.
questions.explanation: A hash is not encryption: there is no key and nothing to decrypt. Guessing works here only because payment notes come from a small set.

questions.question_stem: Anyone can see a suspect's public key. Why can they not spend the suspect's coins with it?
questions.correct_answer: Going back from the public key to the private key is the discrete logarithm problem, which no known computer solves.
incorrect_answers: The public key is a hash of the private key, so spending would mean undoing that hash, which cannot be done.
The public key holds the private key in encrypted form, and only the wallet's own password can open that form.
A node refuses any spend made with a public key on view, so only the holder of the private key can ever spend it.
questions.explanation: Going from key to public key is quick; going back is the discrete logarithm problem, infeasible for secp256k1. Whoever holds the private key can spend, and the public key does not give it up.

questions.question_stem: Sony signed PlayStation 3 software with the same ECDSA nonce each time. What went wrong, and what did it expose?
questions.correct_answer: A nonce must never repeat; two signatures made with one nonce let the private key be worked out.
incorrect_answers: A nonce must differ for each message; two signatures that shared one exposed only the public key.
The curve was too small; with two signatures from one nonce, the private key was found by a search.
The nonce was never hashed first, so each signature held for any message; no key was exposed.
questions.explanation: The algorithm was sound; the use was not. Reusing a signing nonce exposes the private key, as the PlayStation 3 case showed in 2010.

questions.question_stem: A transaction was signed by the key behind address X, one of an exchange's wallets. What may the analyst write?
questions.correct_answer: "Signed with the key controlling address X"; the customer who asked for the withdrawal is a separate fact.
incorrect_answers: "The exchange's customer sent the funds", since a signature from an exchange wallet names that customer by name.
"Smith sent the funds", once the exchange confirms Smith owns that account, because the signature names him.
"No one approved it", since an exchange signs for its customers and a key held by a service proves nothing.
questions.explanation: A signature proves approval was made with the key, not who held it. A service such as an exchange holds keys and signs for its customers, so the customer is a separate fact from the exchange's records.

specific_source.anchor: A signature authorizes; it doesn't identify

questions.question_stem: A user's wallet private key is stolen. What does the lesson say about cancelling that key?
questions.correct_answer: No one can cancel a stolen key; it keeps working until the coins have moved, so a theft looks like any spend.
incorrect_answers: The network blacklists it once the theft is reported, and nodes then reject any later signature from it.
The owner revokes it through the wallet's issuer, as a certificate authority revokes a stolen certificate.
It lapses after the next block, because each signature is checked against a nonce that has moved on.
questions.explanation: Blockchains have no way to revoke a stolen key. It keeps working until the coins move, and on chain a theft looks like any other signed transaction.

specific_source.anchor: Keys fail through people and bad randomness

questions.question_stem: The phone's signature checks, and the phone belongs to Smith. What can the analyst write, and how sure?
questions.correct_answer: "Signed with the key found on Smith's phone", High; whether Smith signed it needs evidence from outside the chain.
incorrect_answers: "Smith signed it", at High confidence, since the signature checks and the phone is Smith's own to use freely.
"Signed with the key found on Smith's phone", at Low confidence, since anyone could have forged the check on the phone.
"Smith signed it", at Moderate confidence, since the phone is Smith's but others may have used its key.
questions.explanation: The confidence word belongs to the key claim, which anyone can repeat the check for. Whether Smith signed is a separate question: the key could have been copied, shared or used by someone else.

questions.question_stem: A classic Bitcoin address has never spent. Can an analyst read its public key from the chain?
questions.correct_answer: No: only the hash of the key is on chain, until the address spends and the transaction shows the key.
incorrect_answers: Yes: a classic address is the public key itself in Base58Check, so the key reads from the first deposit.
No: the key stays hidden even after a spend, because nodes check the address against a hash in the block.
Yes: the Base58Check checksum encodes the public key, so an analyst can decode it with no spend at all.
questions.explanation: A classic address is the hash160 of the public key, so it hides the key. The key and signature appear only when the address spends, and nodes hash the key to check it matches.

questions.question_stem: Why can an Ethereum address have no private key behind it?
questions.correct_answer: A contract has an address too, but its code controls it, so no private key is behind it.
incorrect_answers: Some addresses come from a public key alone, which a wallet can hold with no key behind it.
A fresh address is made per new payment, so most are never linked to any private key at all.
A deployer's key controls every contract's address for good, so only that key is behind each.
questions.explanation: A contract is a program stored on the chain. It has an address, but no private key controls it; its code does, so not every address has a key behind it.

questions.question_stem: In the phone's worked example, which row is secret, and why can anyone check the rest?
questions.correct_answer: Only the private key; anyone with the public key can recompute the addresses and check the signature.
incorrect_answers: Only the signature's s value; the rest follows from r and the public key, which anyone can derive alone.
The private key and the nonce; the addresses and signature need both, so only the signer can repeat them.
The Ethereum address; a Bitcoin address and a signature can be recomputed, but Keccak-256 cannot.
questions.explanation: Only the first row is secret. Anyone with the public key can recompute or check every other row, and no one can work back to the private key.

questions.question_stem: A wallet app lists addresses A (Bitcoin), B (Ethereum) and C (Ethereum). A and B recompute from the phone's key; C does not. What is the finding?
questions.correct_answer: A and B come from the phone's key, High, since anyone can recompute them; another key controls C.
incorrect_answers: A, B and C all belong to the phone's owner, at High, since one wallet app holds all three addresses.
A and B come from the phone's key, Moderate, since the app only lists them; C is on another chain.
Only B comes from the phone's key, since an Ethereum one can be, but a Bitcoin one cannot.
questions.explanation: Recomputing is the evidence: hash160 and Base58Check give A, the last 20 bytes of Keccak-256 give B. C matches neither, so another key controls it. High, because the arithmetic can be repeated.

questions.question_stem: A node receives a signed Ethereum transaction whose value was changed after signing. What happens?
questions.correct_answer: The signature fails, since it covers every field, so the node refuses the transaction.
incorrect_answers: The node accepts it, because the signature covers the sender's key and nonce, not the value.
The node accepts it, because the value is checked only against the sender's balance, no more.
The node refuses it, because a changed value gives a new nonce that the sender already used.
questions.explanation: The signature covers all the signed fields: to, value, nonce and chain ID. Change any field and the signature fails.

questions.question_stem: In the recorded run, the signing page sends the node the signed bytes. What does the node never see?
questions.correct_answer: The private key: it receives only the signed bytes, checks them and returns the transaction hash.
incorrect_answers: The nonce: the node works it out for itself from the pool, so the signed bytes leave it out entirely.
The signature: the node checks the hash alone, since the signed bytes carry only the fields.
The chain ID: the node adds it on receipt, so the signed bytes carry no mention of chain.
questions.explanation: Signing happens before sending. The node gets the signed bytes, never the private key, and hands back the transaction hash.

questions.question_stem: An explorer shows an Ethereum transaction's From address. Where did it come from?
questions.correct_answer: Each node recovered the public key from the signature and hash, then hashed it into the address.
incorrect_answers: The sender typed it into the From field, and the node then checked it against the signature.
The node looked it up in a table that matches each account's nonce to the sender's address.
The address is carried inside r and s, so the node reads it out, as it reads the chain ID.
questions.explanation: A signed Ethereum transaction does not carry the sender's address. The node recovers the public key from the signature and hash, then takes the last 20 bytes of its Keccak-256 hash.

questions.question_stem: Seat 39's signed transaction used nonce 1 and was mined in block 89. Someone copies its signed bytes and sends them to the node again. Which field is the reason for refusal?
questions.correct_answer: The nonce: nonce 1 is used, and changing it would break the signature that covers it.
incorrect_answers: The chain ID: the copy was made for another chain, and the node checks it when it arrives.
The value: the signature lapses an hour after the block, so the value is checked again.
The nonce: nonce 1 is used, but the copier can raise it to 2, as the signature skips it.
questions.explanation: Nonce 1 is already used by seat 39, so the node refuses a second transaction with it, and the copier cannot change the nonce without breaking the signature.

questions.question_stem: A tip says a Bitcoin address belongs to Smith. What does the tip prove, and how sure should the analyst be that Smith controls it?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing about Smith: an address carries no name, so Low that Smith controls it, on a tip alone.
incorrect_answers: That Smith controls the address, at High, since a tip names the address and it is public.
That Smith controls it, at Moderate, since a tip and a public address settle most cases.
That Smith once used the address, Moderate, since a tip is one line of evidence in a case.
questions.explanation: An address is a hash of a public key and carries no name, so a tip alone is Low. Recomputing the address from a key found on Smith's device would make the key link High.

questions.question_stem: In the lab, a student says, "I typed seat 39's address into the From field." What do you tell them?
questions.correct_answer: There is no From field to type into; the node recovered seat 39's address from the signature.
incorrect_answers: That is allowed, but a typed From must match the signature or the node refuses the transaction.
That is allowed when the nonce matches, because From is a signed field, like the value is.
There is no From field; the node copies it from the account's previous transaction in history.
questions.explanation: The From was never typed; the node recovered it from the signature, so seat 39's key signed it. Which student used the seat is a record outside the chain.
